per_question.user_input: What is the Lifetime Learning Credit and how does it differ from the American Opportunity Credit?
per_question.response:
## The Lifetime Learning Credit and How It Differs from the American Opportunity Credit

### What Is the Lifetime Learning Credit?

The Lifetime Learning Credit is one of two tax credits available to help offset the costs of higher education by reducing the amount of income tax you owe [p970, pp.22-23]. For the tax year, you may be able to claim a lifetime learning credit of **up to $2,000** for qualified education expenses paid for all eligible students [p970, pp.22-23].

Importantly, the Lifetime Learning Credit is a **nonrefundable credit**. This means it can reduce your tax to zero, but if the credit is more than your tax, the excess will **not** be refunded to you [p970, p.23].

There is **no limit on the number of years** the Lifetime Learning Credit can be claimed for each student [p970, pp.22-23].

### Key Differences from the American Opportunity Credit

1. **Number of Years You Can Claim the Credit:**
   - **American Opportunity Credit:** You can claim it for the same student for **no more than 4 tax years** [p970, p.23].
   - **Lifetime Learning Credit:** There is **no limit** on the number of years it can be claimed for the same student [p970, p.23].

2. **Credit Amount:**
   - When eligible for both credits for the same student, the **American Opportunity Credit will always be greater** than the Lifetime Learning Credit [p970, p.23].

3. **You Cannot Claim Both for the Same Student in the Same Year:**
   - For each student, you can elect only **one** of the credits per year. For example, if you claim the Lifetime Learning Credit for a child on your 2024 return, you cannot also claim the American Opportunity Credit for that same child in 2024 [p970, p.23].

4. **Applying Credits to Multiple Students:**
   - You can claim different credits for different students in the same year. For example, you can claim the American Opportunity Credit for one student and the Lifetime Learning Credit for another student in the same year [p970, p.23].

5. **Refundability:**
   - The Lifetime Learning Credit is **nonrefundable** (excess credit is not refunded) [p970, p.23], while the American Opportunity Credit has a partially refundable component.

### Practical Tip

If you are eligible to claim both credits for the same student in the same year, you may choose either one — but **not both**. If you have the choice, the American Opportunity Credit will generally be the better option since it will always result in a larger credit [p970, p.10].

per_question.user_input: Are prizes and contest winnings taxable income?
per_question.response:
Yes, prizes and contest winnings are generally taxable income. Here is a detailed breakdown:

## General Rule
If you win a prize in a lucky number drawing, television or radio quiz program, beauty contest, or other event, you must include it in your income. For example, if you win a $50 prize in a photography contest, you must report this income on Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 8i [Pub 17, p.79] [Pub 525, p.36].

## Non-Cash Prizes
Prizes and awards received in goods or services must be included in your income at their **fair market value (FMV)** [Pub 17, p.79] [Pub 525, p.36].

## Refusing a Prize
If you **refuse to accept** a prize, you do not need to include its value in your income [Pub 17, p.79] [Pub 525, p.36].

## Gambling Winnings, Lotteries & Raffles
Gambling winnings — including winnings from lotteries, raffles, and fantasy sports leagues — must be included in your income on Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 8b. In addition to cash, you must also include the FMV of noncash prizes such as bonds, cars, and houses [Pub 17, p.78] [Pub 525, p.34].

## Employee Awards & Bonuses
Cash awards or bonuses given by your employer for good work or suggestions must generally be included in your income as wages. However, certain **noncash employee achievement awards** can be excluded from income [Pub 17, p.79] [Pub 525, p.36].

## Prize Points (Salespeople)
If you are a salesperson and receive prize points redeemable for merchandise, you must include their FMV in your income. These are taxable in the year they are paid or made available to you, not when you redeem them [Pub 525, p.36].

## Scholarship Contest Prizes
Scholarship prizes won in a contest are **not** considered scholarships or fellowships if you are not required to use them for educational purposes. You must include these amounts in your income on Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 8i, regardless of whether you use them for educational purposes [Pub 525, p.37].

## Pulitzer, Nobel, and Similar Prizes
If you receive a prize for accomplishments in religious, charitable, scientific, artistic, educational, literary, or civic fields, you must generally include its value in your income. However, you may **exclude** the prize if **all** of the following conditions are met [Pub 17, p.79] [Pub 525, p.36]:
1. You were selected without any action on your part to enter the contest or proceeding.
2. You are not required to perform substantial future services as a condition for receiving the prize or award.
3. The prize or award is transferred by the payer **directly** to a governmental unit or tax-exempt charitable organization as designated by you (and you cannot use it before it is transferred) [Pub 525, p.36].

In summary, prizes and contest winnings are broadly taxable, whether received in cash or as noncash items valued at FMV, with only narrow exceptions such as declined prizes or qualifying transfers of certain prestigious awards to charity.

Chapter 8 Other Income

Gambling winnings. You must include your
gambling winnings in your income on Schedule
1 (Form 1040), line 8b. Winnings from fantasy
sports leagues are gambling winnings. If you
itemize your deductions on Schedule A (Form
1040), you can deduct gambling losses you had
during the year, but only up to the amount of
your winnings. If you're in the trade or business
of gambling, use Schedule C (Form 1040). For

tax years 2018 through 2025, professional gam-
bling losses and expenses are limited to the
amount of your winnings.
Lotteries and raffles. Winnings from lotter-
ies and raffles are gambling winnings. In addi-
tion to cash winnings, you must include in your
income the FMV of bonds, cars, houses, and
other noncash prizes. However, the difference
between the FMV and the cost of an oil and gas

lease obtained from the government through a
lottery isn't includible in income.

nual payments and any amounts you receive
designated as interest on the unpaid install-
ments. If you sell future lottery payments for a
lump sum, you must report the amount you re-

ceive from the sale as ordinary income (on
Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 8b) in the year
you receive it.

per_question.reference: Yes. Prizes and awards are generally included in gross income and are fully taxable at their fair market value, whether received as cash, merchandise, or trips. You must report the fair market value as income. An exception applies to certain employee achievement awards given as tangible personal property within dollar limits. See IRS Publication 525.
